newsitem.title: MEXICO: Drug scandals come as no surprise to Mexicans.
newsitem.headline: Drug scandals come as no surprise to Mexicans.

text.p: Reeling from one big drug scandal after another, Mexicans agreed on Monday on one thing: news about traffickers' links to top government officals came as no surprise.

Allegations by the New York Times that two state governors were tied to drug lords dominated newspaper front pages days after Mexico arrested its top drugs fighter on corruption charges and following sensational stories alleging that former President Carlos Salinas and his family received money and favours from drug lords during his 1988-94 administration.
In each scandal, all of the accused denied strongly the charges against them, but analysts said most of the recent revelations had been circulating as gossip for a long time.

"What are we surprised about?" asked managing editor Raymundo Riva Palacio in a column in Reforma newspaper. After listing a long series of drug scandals going back more than a decade, he said the real problem was "the tolerance, complacency and collusion of the Mexican state with the drug traffickers."

U.S. drug officials say more than 70 percent of the cocaine entering their country comes through Mexico, which is also home to several of the world's most powerful drug cartels and a major producer of marijuana and heroin.

Roberto Rock, director of El Universal daily, said Mexican newspapers previously had mentioned accusations against the two governors fingered by the Times, in particular Sonora leader Manlio Fabio Beltrones. But he said Mexican papers gave Page One play to the allegations on Sunday because it allowed them to give the charges prominence without taking responsibility for them.

Diplomats also were not surprised by the allegations but noted that the U.S. and Mexican governments had tried to keep Mexico's failings in the drug war out of the headlines. While the United States has long been happy to lecture Colombia, Peru or Panama publicly about their failings in the war on drugs, Mexico has always received a pat on the back.

U.S. Ambassador to Mexico James Jones never lost a chance to extol the virtues of the Mexican government, laud its commitment to the war on drugs and sing the praises of top officials like former Attorney-General Antonio Lozano, fired last December amid charges of evidence-rigging and bribery of witnesses, and disgraced anti-drug czar Gen. Jesus Gutierrez Rebollo.

"What the Clinton administration has failed to understand is that the Mexican system is hopelessly, most likely irredeemably, corrupt," Mexican commentator Jorge Castaneda said in an article for Newsweek magazine.
"The Americans continue to hope that by nudging this rotten giant it will gradually change for the better," he wrote.

Political analyst Jose Antonio Crespo said he thought the New York Times story, which he said appeared to be based mostly on leaks from Drug Enforcement Administration (DEA) officials in the United States, might be intended to encourage Zedillo to put more pressure on politicians suspected of drug links.

"I think the United States sees old-guard politicians suspected of links to drug traffickers gaining ground and Zedillo not doing anything about it ... so they put pressure on him to react," Crespo told Reuters.
